strengths: SGDRO addresses an important computer vision problem: maintaining accuracy on minority groups under distribution shift. Combining a pooled-loss SAM perturbation with adversarial group reweighting is simple, potentially useful, and specified in Algorithm 1.

The controlled Waterbirds comparison provides encouraging evidence. With the same strong weight penalty and five random seeds, SGDRO improves worst-group accuracy over GDRO from 86.5% to 87.2% and group-average accuracy from 90.4% to 90.6%, improving both minority groups.

Evaluation extends beyond Waterbirds to six DomainBed datasets, using training-domain validation and three random seeds. SGDRO achieves 71.4% average accuracy versus 70.1% for GDRO and 70.9% for ERM, supporting some usefulness for domain generalization.

Table 2 provides evidence of reduced local curvature: SGDRO lowers both leading Hessian eigenvalues in every Waterbirds group relative to GDRO under the same weight penalty. The overall largest eigenvalue decreases from 356.6 to 268.7.
weaknesses: The central guarantees are not established. Section 3.1 supplies only a local Taylor argument and uses pooled-loss derivatives where the fixed-group update requires ∇L_g + ρH_g∇L_S/||∇L_S||. Equation (4) also depends on θ through ε*, whereas Algorithm 1 omits this derivative without analyzing the approximation. Correcting the notation would not establish convergence, common flat minima, or worst-group generalization. In particular, an ascent direction for pooled loss need not maximize an individual group's neighborhood loss.

The added value of the specific combination is insufficiently isolated. There is no ablation comparing the proposed pooled-loss perturbation with perturbations computed from the worst-group or adversarially weighted loss. DomainBed omits SAM, leaving unclear whether group reweighting adds value beyond sharpness-aware training there. On Waterbirds, SAM and SGDRO use weight penalties of 0.0001 and 1.0, respectively, which further limits attribution in that comparison. These omissions matter because the methodological contribution is primarily the coupling of two established methods.

The claimed improvement in the average-versus-worst-group trade-off is not demonstrated by Table 1. The 0.7-point worst-group gain accompanies a weighted-average decline from 93.8% to 93.1%, and both majority groups lose accuracy. This can still be a useful operating point, but it does not substantiate the claim that SGDRO alleviates majority-group performance decreases. Uncertainty for the improvement itself is not reported.

The mechanistic and robustness conclusions exceed the measurements. Table 2 and Figure 2 measure local test-loss curvature; lower eigenvalues do not establish shared stationary minima, smaller train–test generalization gaps, or a causal explanation for improved accuracy. Meanwhile, DomainBed reports average held-out-domain accuracy rather than worst-domain or subgroup accuracy, so the broader evaluation does not directly establish the central worst-case benefit beyond Waterbirds.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the useful pseudocode and references to standard settings. The DomainBed perturbation-radius values or search distribution, Waterbirds checkpoint-selection criterion, and meaning of the ± quantities in Table 1 are not specified. These are correctable reporting issues; the stronger reasons for weak rejection are the unsupported central guarantees and insufficient evidence isolating the proposed design's benefit.
